usedHookFrames: predictably-irrational-ch01: A useless middle choice can make the larger bill feel like the only sensible one.
predictably-irrational-ch02: The first number on the table can become the ruler you never meant to use.
predictably-irrational-ch03: Zero on the tag can make time, clutter, and delay vanish from the bill.
predictably-irrational-ch04: A five-dollar card can turn a generous act into a badly paid job.
predictably-irrational-ch05: The river gauge is easiest to respect before the raft is already in your hands.
predictably-irrational-ch06: A final deadline that waits politely can let the real failure happen weeks early.
predictably-irrational-ch07: The vase gains a second price the moment your initials dry on the base.
predictably-irrational-ch08: The extra prototype does not sit quietly; it eats another test day every week.
predictably-irrational-ch09: The paper around the bow can change what the violinist hears before the first note fades.
predictably-irrational-ch10: Tape over the sticker before your knees decide which insole helped.
predictably-irrational-ch11: The pledge on the wall works best before the raffle cash is counted.
predictably-irrational-ch12: The sticker feels harmless until someone writes six dollars beside the roll.
predictably-irrational-ch13: The first order at the table can make everyone else's appetite sound like a performance.
usedCounterFrames: predictably-irrational-ch01: The option that changes your mind may be the one nobody is meant to choose. A decoy wins by losing clearly, so the favored option can borrow its glow.

predictably-irrational-ch02: Demand can feel personal and coherent even when it grew around an arbitrary anchor. The better move is to build a private estimate before the market names reality for you.
predictably-irrational-ch03: Free does not simply lower the price. It changes the feeling of risk, so the paid option must defend itself while the free option glides past its own costs.
predictably-irrational-ch04: Money does not only add motivation. It can move a moment from reciprocity into exchange, where people ask whether the price is fair instead of whether they want to help.
predictably-irrational-ch05: The calm self is a poor witness for the hot self. Awareness is too light unless the cold state leaves a barrier the aroused state cannot bargain away.

predictably-irrational-ch06: Freedom feels like it protects quality, but it can protect delay. Self-control improves when a distant goal gets earlier checkpoints that can embarrass, block, or correct you before the end.
predictably-irrational-ch07: Ownership looks like proof of value, but it adds loss to the math. Selling asks you to give up a story while buying would ask only what the object can do.
predictably-irrational-ch08: An open option can feel like safety while it drains the option you actually need. The cost is not the loss of the door, but the upkeep spent keeping it unlocked.
predictably-irrational-ch09: Expectations do not merely change what people say afterward. They can enter the experience early, making the cue part of what taste, tone, or quality feels like.
predictably-irrational-ch10: Price can act like an ingredient in expectation. A discount is not always a pure gain if it quietly lowers the result you expect to feel.
predictably-irrational-ch11: Honesty feels like a trait you carry into the room, but the decisive moment is often the cue that appears before the excuse gets comfortable.
predictably-irrational-ch12: Value does not feel equally moral in every costume. A token or voucher can make the same loss feel softer than cash.
predictably-irrational-ch13: Public choice can be less informative than private choice. The cheap fix is often not persuasion, but a quieter way to collect the first preference.
usedTryThisNowFrames: predictably-irrational-ch01: Cover the option that mainly makes another option look good, then ask whether the apparent winner still solves the original need.
predictably-irrational-ch02: Before reading the next price, write one fair number and the reason behind it; let that note meet the quote first.
predictably-irrational-ch03: Choose one free offer and translate it into minutes lost, space used, extra steps, or attention spent before accepting it.
predictably-irrational-ch04: Before paying for a favor, name the norm already carrying the moment; if it is reciprocity, use thanks, status, or care instead of a price.
predictably-irrational-ch05: Pick one state that changes your standards and place a barrier now, such as a lockbox, signed limit, draft rule, or cancellation line.
predictably-irrational-ch06: Choose one deadline more than a week away and create a visible checkpoint within forty-eight hours that proves real progress.
predictably-irrational-ch07: Choose one owned thing you rarely use, hide the ownership cue, and write the most you would pay to buy it today from a stranger.
predictably-irrational-ch08: Name one option you maintain with time or attention, then schedule a closing action unless it has been used in the last month.
predictably-irrational-ch09: Cover one label or maker name long enough to record your first judgment before the cue returns.
predictably-irrational-ch10: Before judging a paid tool or product, hide the price and write one observable result you can compare without knowing the cost.
predictably-irrational-ch11: Move one rule, pledge, or standard to the exact place where the questionable choice begins, before the private excuse starts.
predictably-irrational-ch12: Pick one voucher or shared points balance and write its cash equivalent beside the place where it gets used.
predictably-irrational-ch13: For one group decision this week, collect first preferences privately before discussion, then compare that signal with the public conversation.
usedQuizExplanationFrames: predictably-irrational-ch01: The middle package is built to lose beside the dessert bundle, so it changes the comparison frame. Absolute value would require checking headcount, appetite, and budget, not just t | Hiding the weak middle license tests whether the largest license solves the real research problem. Vendor popularity keeps the seller's frame in charge, and clear dominance over a  | The cramped cabin may be making the spacious one look better than it is. Their real plans are the missing comparison, while scarcity and lake-view logic both stay inside the plante

predictably-irrational-ch02: The $9,000 number became the ruler, so $5,400 feels moderate by comparison. Loss aversion and social norms might matter elsewhere, but the key mechanism is the first price. | A parts-and-hours estimate gives later quotes an independent reference point. Choosing the middle quote still orbits the first number, and rejecting every high quote overcorrects. | The old purchase has become evidence for future purchases, which is self-herding. Fairness still needs current comparables, and donor opinion is not the active mechanism.

predictably-irrational-ch03: The tote's zero price hid inconvenience and space. Paid quality and social obligation could matter in other scenes, but the core failure is not counting the nonmoney bill. | The freelancer needs to translate free into time and opportunity cost. Automatic acceptance ignores the hidden bill, while automatic refusal misses cases where the tradeoff is wort | The free bowl draws attention away from extra spending. The added items are the hidden cost; nothing in the scene proves a real need or a social obligation.

predictably-irrational-ch04: The card can reclassify help as underpaid work. Distraction and card size miss the key switch from social recognition to market pricing. | The rota and public thanks keep the act inside mutual aid. A small fee or token payment risks giving residents a market price for opting out or helping. | The tiny bounty changed how contributors interpreted the work. Skill and task importance did not need to change; the meaning of participation changed.

predictably-irrational-ch05: The calm self mispredicted hot-state judgment near the summit. More data can help, but the central failure is assuming the later state will honor the same line. | A signed maximum and handoff change the later choice. Promises and last-minute decisions leave the competitive state in charge. | The problem is state-dependent judgment during night work. Removing all tasting is too blunt, and the scene does not show a lack of values.

predictably-irrational-ch06: A far deadline can fail to shape today's behavior. Freedom may help some teams, but without proof points, delay can hide until late. | Signed walkthroughs create earlier consequences and evidence. A reminder and general awareness leave too much hidden until the final date. | If drafts surface only at the end, flexibility is shielding delay. Creative work can still use artifacts like outlines, sample pages, or recorded tests.

predictably-irrational-ch07: The gap between selling price and today's buy price points to ownership and loss aversion. Anchoring and social norms are not the main evidence in this scene. | Hiding the signature helps her see the canvas as a buyer would. Labor may matter, but buyers do not automatically pay for every remembered hour. | Ownership makes selling feel like a loss, which inflates the demanded price. The buy price test shows the market value is probably lower.

predictably-irrational-ch08: The key cost is maintenance: testing, bug fixes, and attention. Emotional pain may exist, but it is not the option's ongoing rent. | The director needs to count option upkeep and protect rehearsal quality. Keeping or delaying preserves possibility while spending resources. | The issue is option maintenance, not lack of care. Renewals keep possible paths alive while draining time from current cases.

predictably-irrational-ch09: The chef cue can alter expectation and therefore reported experience. Nothing suggests the soup changed chemically or that the diner is lying. | Numbered samples delay the expectation cue so taste can be recorded first. Asking about rumors or adding a health label keeps expectations active. | The identical code points toward expectation-driven attention. Hidden differences and sabotage are unsupported by the scene.

predictably-irrational-ch10: The sticker may shape expected support before the result is tested. The knee can still matter, and the lesson is not that all expensive products are fake. | Renaming and bouncing separates the audible result from the price cue. Reviews and confidence may matter later, but they do not test what he hears. | Observable counts separate effectiveness from discount-shaped doubt. Price alone should not decide whether the treatment worked.

predictably-irrational-ch11: The issue is rationalized small cheating that preserves self-image. The scene does not require fixed bad character or higher punishment. | The early visible cue interrupts rationalization before the act. Hiding price or delaying checks gives the excuse more room. | The oath belongs before the choice, in the path of action. Scolding afterward is late, and a smaller sheet may make the rule easier to dismiss.

predictably-irrational-ch12: The sticker represents value but feels less like money. That distance makes misuse easier to rationalize; it does not mean the sticker is valueless. | Showing the ticket price translates the credit back into value. Deleting or casually giving credits away both avoid the real moral-distance issue. | The menu-price total restores the value behind the voucher. Trustworthiness and breakfast size do not address the abstraction.

predictably-irrational-ch13: Public ordering adds audience and sequence pressure. The scene does not imply the options were confusing or that private preference is meaningless. | Sealed cards capture first preferences before hierarchy or applause shapes them. Senior nominations and applause add public pressure. | Folded slips protect appetite from bravado and sequence. Making the dish spicier or canceling planning misses the preference-performance problem.
